overview.title: 📖 Overview: Counting Violations, Then a New Mishna
overview.subtitle: Temurah 7a–7b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין הַכֹּהֲנִים מְמִירִין לֹא בְּחַטָּאת וְלֹא בְּאָשָׁם וְלֹא בִּבְכוֹר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes the blemished-animal discussion: Reish Lakish questions whether the five prohibitions apply only to an animal that became blemished after consecration, or even one blemished from birth, likening the latter to a worthless date palm; Rabbi Yoḥanan replies that consecrating a born-blemished animal is disgraceful precisely because superior animals were available. Abaye and Rava then dispute whether burning a whole blemished offering and burning part of one count as one violation or two. The daf then introduces a new mishna: priests and Israelites each substitute only for their own offerings, and priests cannot substitute for a sin offering, guilt offering, or firstborn they received as a gift — with Rabbi Akiva grounding the rule in temurah's own verse, which requires that sanctity take hold 'in the house of the owner.'

slides.title: 🌴 Is a Born-Blemished Animal Like a Date Palm?
slides.subtitle: Reish Lakish challenges whether all five prohibitions really apply equally

lines.speaker: Reish Lakish
lines.text: Perhaps the five prohibitions apply only to an animal that became blemished after being fit. One consecrated blemished from birth is like consecrating a mere date palm — his real intent is its value, which is permitted!

lines.speaker: R' Ḥiyya bar Yosef
lines.text: But the verse itself lists שָׂרוּעַ וְקָלוּט — 'too long or too short' — congenital blemishes, right in the passage of prohibition!

lines.speaker: Rabbi Yoḥanan
lines.text: The real difference is disgrace (בִּזְיָא מִילְּתָא): a date palm was never a candidate for the altar at all. But this person had unblemished animals available and chose a blemished one instead — that is what makes him liable.

lines.speaker: Rava adds
lines.text: If disgrace is the reason, then even one who consecrates it explicitly for its value, to buy libations, should be flogged too — the act itself remains disgraceful.

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: A baraita is found supporting Rava: consecrating a blemished animal even 'for a gift' (i.e., for Temple upkeep) is included in the prohibition, not just consecration as an altar offering.

slides.title: ✋ One Act, How Many Lashes?
slides.subtitle: Abaye and Rava dispute whether burning 'all' and burning 'part' are one violation or two
rows: Burning all of a blemished offering and burning part of it are two distinct prohibitions
Two sets of lashes for one act
One cannot be flogged twice for a single general prohibition (לָאו שֶׁבִּכְלָלוֹת) drawn from one verse
The Tosefta's list of five separate violations already counts both 'all' and 'part' as distinct items
Attempts to reread the baraita in Abaye's favor fail

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: This dispute sharpens exactly how the five (or six) prohibitions of blemished consecration are counted and applied.

slides.title: 🐑🐐 New Mishna: Who Substitutes for What?
slides.subtitle: Priests and Israelites each substitute for their own consecrated animals

nodes.content: 📜 Mishna: priests substitute for their own offerings; Israelites for theirs. Priests do NOT substitute for a sin offering, guilt offering, or firstborn they received
❓ R' Yoḥanan ben Nuri: why not the firstborn? Unlike sin/guilt offerings, priests DO acquire a firstborn during its lifetime, while it is still with the Israelite owner!
💬 R' Akiva: 'both it and its substitute shall be holy' — sanctity must take hold in the house of the (original) owner
✅ Since the firstborn was never consecrated in the priest's house — it was born already sacred, in the Israelite's house — the priest cannot be the one to substitute for it

callout.label: Key verse:
callout.text: הוּא וּתְמוּרָתוֹ יִהְיֶה קֹּדֶשׁ — the same phrase used throughout the tractate now anchors a rule about whose 'ownership' substitution requires.

slides.title: 🏠 Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri vs. Rabbi Akiva
slides.subtitle: Same mishna, two different lenses on 'ownership'

boxes.title: R' Yoḥanan ben Nuri
items: Priests acquire a firstborn during its life, unlike sin/guilt offerings
Sees no reason to equate the firstborn with sin/guilt offerings

boxes.title: Rabbi Akiva
items: Focuses on where sanctity first took hold
A firstborn's sanctity begins automatically at birth, in the Israelite's home
Only the person in whose house consecration happened can substitute — so the priest cannot

callout.label: Halakhic outcome:
callout.text: Priests cannot substitute for a sin offering, guilt offering, or firstborn received from an Israelite, though the reasoning differs between the two tanna'im.

slides.title: 💰 Selling an Unblemished Firstborn: Now or When the Temple Stood?
slides.subtitle: Rav Naḥman and Rava argue over a mishna about firstborn sales

lines.speaker: Mishna
lines.text: A firstborn offering may be sold unblemished only while alive; if blemished, alive or slaughtered. A priest may betroth a woman with it.

lines.speaker: Rav Naḥman
lines.text: This applies only nowadays, with no Temple, since the priest fully owns it. When the Temple stands, an unblemished firstborn is destined for the altar — it may not be sold alive at all!

lines.speaker: Rava objects
lines.text: But if the mishna limits the sale to 'while alive,' implying not once slaughtered — that only makes sense when the Temple stands, since nowadays a firstborn is never slaughtered as an offering at all!

lines.speaker: Rav Naḥman clarifies
lines.text: The mishna is still about nowadays; it isn't excluding a slaughtered case, just teaching that even today one may sell it alive.

callout.label: Point at stake:
callout.text: Whether a priest's ownership of an unblemished firstborn is full ownership (allowing sale) even while the Temple stands and the animal awaits sacrifice.

summary.principle: Consecrating a blemished animal is disgraceful regardless of whether the blemish is congenital or acquired, and temurah's requirement that sanctity take hold 'in the house of the owner' explains why a priest cannot substitute for a sin offering, guilt offering, or firstborn received from an Israelite.

flowSteps.content: 🌴 Reish Lakish questions congenital blemishes; R' Yoḥanan: disgrace applies regardless
✋ Abaye vs. Rava: one violation or two for burning 'all' vs. 'part'? Rava's view prevails

columns.content: 🐑🐐 New mishna: priests/Israelites substitute only for their own offerings
🏠 R' Akiva: sanctity — and temurah — must occur in the owner's house

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: substitution requires that the substituter be the one in whose domain the original consecration occurred

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, why is one flogged for consecrating an animal that was blemished from birth, even though this differs from consecrating a mere date palm?
o: Because animals are always more valuable than plants
Because it is disgraceful (בִּזְיָא) — he had unblemished animals of the same kind available and chose a blemished one
Because date palms cannot be consecrated at all
Because the Torah never mentions blemished animals
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that a date palm was never a candidate for the altar to begin with, but an animal blemished from birth is disgraceful specifically because unblemished animals of its kind exist and were passed over.

quiz.q: In the dispute over burning a whole blemished offering vs. part of it, whose opinion does the Gemara ultimately uphold?
o: Abaye's — only one violation, since it's a general prohibition from one verse
Rava's — two distinct violations, since the Tosefta counts them separately
Neither — both are rejected
Rabbi Akiva's
quiz.e: The Gemara concludes תְּיוּבְתָּא (a conclusive refutation) of Abaye's position, based on the Tosefta's list treating 'burning all' and 'burning part' as two separate named violations.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, which offerings can a priest NOT substitute for?
o: Any offering whatsoever
A sin offering, a guilt offering, and a firstborn offering received from an Israelite
Only burnt offerings
Only offerings brought by women
quiz.e: The mishna states that priests do not effect substitution for a sin offering, guilt offering, or firstborn, since these come to them as gifts rather than through their own consecration.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Akiva prove that a priest cannot substitute for a firstborn he received, using temurah's own verse?
o: He cites a verse about teruma instead
'Both it and its substitute shall be holy' implies sanctity must take hold in the house of the original owner — which for a firstborn is the Israelite, not the priest
He says priests can never perform any mitzva involving animals
He argues the firstborn is never truly consecrated
quiz.e: Rabbi Akiva reads 'הוּא וּתְמוּרָתוֹ' as requiring that the substitute be created by the same person in whose house the original consecration occurred — for a firstborn, that is the Israelite's house, not the priest's.

quiz.q: According to Rav Naḥman, when does the halakha permitting sale of an unblemished firstborn while alive apply?
o: Only when the Temple stands
Only in the present era, when there is no Temple and the priest fully owns it
Never — it is always forbidden
Only to blemished firstborns
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman limits this ruling to the present, without a Temple, since when the Temple stood an unblemished firstborn was destined for the altar and could not be sold alive at all.
